prohibited_recommendations: Do not order prolonged rhythm monitoring when a structural embolic source has already been demonstrated and the treatment decision is settled
Do not continue aspirin alongside a new anticoagulant without a specific coronary indication
Do not administer iodinated contrast studies in a patient with a documented contrast allergy without premedication and a clear indication
Do not treat this as small-vessel disease on a Fazekas 1-2 burden
Do not leave a newly identified ejection fraction of 38% unaddressed
required_recommendations: Establish the stepwise course and date each step
Recognise that an old anterior infarction in a patient with multi-territory brain infarcts is a structural embolic question
Obtain an ECG, and when it shows sinus rhythm with an old anterior infarct, proceed to echocardiography rather than to rhythm monitoring
Obtain brain MRI, count the infarcts by territory, and check SWI before anticoagulating
Image the carotid arteries to exclude a large-artery mechanism
Anticoagulate for the demonstrated left ventricular thrombus and stop the antiplatelet in the absence of a separate indication
Refer for heart failure management of an ejection fraction of 38%

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on

The embolic source has been identified structurally — an apical aneurysm with mural thrombus — and the indication to anticoagulate follows from it; documenting an arrhythmia would not change the decision already made

accepted: Vascular dementia — multi-infarct type, cardioembolic from a left ventricular apical aneurysm with mural thrombus after an unrecognised anterior myocardial infarction

differential.key_features: A reasonable hypothesis in a multi-territory pattern, but a structural source has been demonstrated — an apical aneurysm with laminated thrombus — and the ECG shows no atrial ectopy, so further rhythm monitoring would not change management
Stepwise course with dateable events, cue-responsive recall and preserved hippocampi
Fazekas 1-2 burden is far below the threshold for attributing a dementia to small-vessel disease
No significant carotid disease, and no single artery supplies three territories across both circulations
No fever, no murmur of regurgitation beyond mild functional mitral regurgitation, no vegetation on echocardiography and no systemic features

key_clinical_evidence: Cardioembolism is not synonymous with atrial fibrillation: an akinetic apical aneurysm with mural thrombus after an anterior infarct is an embolic source in a patient in sinus rhythm
The infarct distribution across both circulations forces the search for a proximal source, and the ECG points the search toward structure rather than rhythm
A silent myocardial infarction found incidentally and never investigated is the omission this case is built on — the echocardiogram it should have prompted is the study that makes the diagnosis
Once a structural source is demonstrated, rhythm monitoring adds cost without changing management
Checking SWI before anticoagulation is part of the decision, not an afterthought

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Lucia Ferraro is a 77-year-old retired seamstress who lives alone and attends with her son. He describes two abrupt worsenings over eighteen months. The first, about eighteen months ago, followed a morning when she was found confused and unable to name objects for a few hours; no medical attention was sought. The second, seven months ago, was a day of clumsiness of the left hand that lasted two days. After each event she was permanently worse: she now cannot manage her own medication, has left the door unlocked repeatedly, and no longer sews, which she had done professionally. Between the events she was stable. Her memory improves with prompting about context. Three years ago an ECG performed before a dental procedure showed an old anterior infarction that she had never known about; no echocardiogram or further cardiac assessment followed. She has no chest pain, no dyspnoea on exertion beyond her usual, and no palpitations. Her pulse is regular. She has never had documented atrial fibrillation. She is allergic to iodinated contrast. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuations and no dream enactment.
